name: VC Funding Frenzy
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Reading the Venture Cycle Like You'd Read Any Other Bubble
lesson.summary: Venture funding into quantum computing has followed a recognizable hype-cycle pattern, a SPAC-driven public listing wave, a funding pullback, and renewed interest, and recognizing that pattern beats taking either the boosters' or the doomsayers' read on any single funding round.
lesson.body:
Venture capital funding into quantum computing did not arrive as a steady stream. It came in a recognizable boom, pullback, and rebound pattern that closely mirrors how VC money has historically flowed into other pre-revenue deep-tech sectors, biotech genomics in the early 2000s, clean energy roughly between 2007 and 2011, and more recently generative AI. Recognizing this pattern matters because each phase gets narrated very differently by people with something to sell: unstoppable momentum during the boom, the bubble has burst during the pullback, neither of which is a rigorous investment read on its own.

The most visible marker of the quantum funding frenzy was the 2021-2022 wave of SPAC, or special purpose acquisition company, mergers that took several quantum computing hardware companies, including IonQ, Rigetti Computing, and D-Wave, public well before any of them had meaningful commercial revenue. SPACs were, at that moment, a popular route for pre-revenue technology companies across many sectors to reach public markets faster and with more flexible forward-looking projections than a traditional IPO allows, and quantum computing rode that same wave alongside the broader 2020 to 2021 boom in speculative technology investing.

What followed was a familiar pullback. Broader venture funding tightened considerably from 2022 onward as interest rates rose, which mechanically raises the risk-free rate underlying every risk-adjusted-return calculation in this book and lowers the present value of long-dated payoffs, exactly as the NPV chapter demonstrated with actual numbers. Quantum computing funding rounds, alongside speculative technology funding generally, cooled noticeably from their 2021 peak. This is exactly what the expected-value framework predicts investors do when the risk-free alternative becomes more attractive: the bar every quantum computing bet has to clear rises automatically, without the underlying technology changing at all.

The frenzy pattern matters for a specific, practical reason connected to both opportunity cost and the sunk cost trap. Capital deployed at the top of a hype cycle, when valuations are richest and diligence is often weakest, systematically earns worse risk-adjusted returns than the same capital deployed during a cooler, more disciplined funding environment, simply because the price paid per unit of genuine technical progress is higher at the peak. Investors who wrote checks into quantum computing startups in 2021 at boom-era valuations need considerably more eventual commercial success to hit the same ROI as investors writing similarly sized checks into similar technology during a calmer, lower-valuation later round.

None of this makes venture enthusiasm for quantum computing irrational as a category. The expected-value logic from earlier in this book, a portfolio of mostly losing bets justified by a small chance of an enormous winner, is a legitimate model for investing in genuinely transformative, uncertain technology. But recognizing the frenzy for what it is, a cyclical, sentiment-driven funding pattern layered on top of a slow-moving, decades-long technology maturation curve, is what separates a disciplined investor asking whether this specific round at this specific valuation is still expected-value positive from one simply riding the narrative up and, inevitably, back down.
